topics.title: Describing motion: position, path length and displacement

learn.hook: A Mumbai local covers 30 km in a day and ends up back at Churchgate. Did it 'go' anywhere? Physics answers both yes and no.
points: Motion is the change of position of an object with time. Rectilinear motion is motion along a straight line.
An object can be treated as a point object when its size is much smaller than the distance it moves (a car on a 200 km trip).
Kinematics describes motion (position, velocity, acceleration) without asking what causes it.
Choose an origin O and a positive direction on the x-axis. Positions to the right are positive, to the left negative; displacement Δx = x₂ − x₁ can be positive, negative or zero.
Path length is the total distance travelled (always positive). Average velocity = Δx/Δt; average speed = path length/time. Average speed ≥ magnitude of average velocity.

example.q: A cyclist goes from x = 0 to x = +500 m and then returns to x = +300 m, taking 100 s in all. Find path length, displacement, average speed and average velocity.

learn.reallife: A runner completing one lap of a 400 m track at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium has a path length of 400 m but zero displacement.

games.title: Displacement or distance?
items: Displacement can be zero even when path length is not.
A round trip ends where it began.
Path length can be smaller than the magnitude of displacement.
Kinematics studies the causes of motion.
Causes are studied in dynamics (laws of motion).
A train on a 1000 km journey can be treated as a point object.
Its length is tiny compared with the distance.
Average speed equals the magnitude of average velocity only if the motion is in one direction without turning back.

quiz.q: A car moves from x = +40 m to x = −20 m. Its displacement in metres is
quiz.explain: Δx = x₂ − x₁ = −20 − 40 = −60 m. The minus sign shows motion in the −x direction.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order or drops the sign

quiz.q: A person walks 60 m east and then 20 m west along the same straight road in 40 s. The average speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: Average speed = path length/time = (60 + 20)/40 = 2 m s⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Uses displacement instead of path length

quiz.q: For the same walk (60 m east, then 20 m west in 40 s), the magnitude of average velocity in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: Displacement = 60 − 20 = 40 m east, so average velocity = 40/40 = 1 m s⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Uses total distance instead of displacement

quiz.q: An athlete completes exactly one round of a 400 m circular track in 50 s. The average velocity is
quiz.explain: The athlete returns to the start, so displacement and hence average velocity are zero. (Average speed is 8 m s⁻¹.)
quiz.mistake: Confuses average speed with average velocity

quiz.q: In which case can the object be treated as a point object?
options: A wheel rolling on a road, studying its spin
A cricket ball spinning about its axis
The Earth revolving around the Sun
A door rotating on its hinges
quiz.explain: The Earth's size is tiny compared with its orbit, so for orbital motion it can be treated as a point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only small objects can be point objects

quiz.q: Kinematics is the study of
quiz.explain: Kinematics describes how things move; dynamics explains why.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up kinematics with dynamics

quiz.q: If the origin is shifted, which quantity remains unchanged for a given motion?
options: Both position and the sign of position
quiz.explain: Displacement Δx = x₂ − x₁ is a difference, so shifting the origin changes both x values equally and Δx stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks displacement depends on where the origin is

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The average speed of a body can be greater than the magnitude of its average velocity.
Reason (R): Path length is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Average speed uses path length and average velocity uses displacement over the same time, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks speed and velocity always have equal magnitudes

teach.ask: Gappu flew 2 km around a tree and landed back on the same branch. He says he 'moved 2 km'. Explain path length, displacement and the role of the origin.
teach.praise: So I flew 2 km but my displacement is zero! Physics is sneaky.
teach.nudge: What is the difference between total distance and change in position? What is your displacement if you return to start?

learn.hook: A speed camera on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway doesn't care about your average for the trip; it measures your velocity at one instant.
points: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero: v = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt.
On a position–time graph, v at an instant is the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point.
Numerical approach: compute Δx/Δt for smaller and smaller Δt; the values approach v (e.g. x = 0.1t³ gives 1.9, 1.261, 1.206 … → 1.2 m s⁻¹ at t = 2 s).
Instantaneous speed = magnitude of instantaneous velocity. But average speed over an interval can exceed the magnitude of average velocity.

example.q: For x = 0.1t³ (x in m, t in s), find Δx/Δt from t = 2 s to t = 2.1 s, and the instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s.

learn.reallife: A car's speedometer shows instantaneous speed, while the trip computer on the same dashboard shows average speed.

games.title: Shrinking intervals for x = 0.1t³ near t = 2 s
games.prompt: Arrange Δx/Δt values from largest Δt to smallest Δt

games.title: Instantaneous velocity
items: Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent to the x–t graph.
Instantaneous speed is always equal to the magnitude of instantaneous velocity.
For a single instant they are equal.
Average speed over an interval is always equal to the magnitude of average velocity.
Not if the object turns back.
A horizontal tangent on an x–t graph means zero velocity at that instant.
Instantaneous velocity can be found only from a formula, never from a graph.
The slope of the tangent gives it.

quiz.q: Instantaneous velocity is defined as
options: The limit of Δx/Δt as Δt → 0
quiz.explain: v = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt.
quiz.mistake: Uses the definition of average speed or acceleration

quiz.q: On a position–time graph, the instantaneous velocity at a point is given by
options: The slope of the chord from the origin
The slope of the tangent at that point
quiz.explain: The tangent's slope is the limit of chord slopes as the interval shrinks.
quiz.mistake: Uses the chord slope (average velocity) or area

quiz.q: For x = 0.1t³ (SI units), the average velocity from t = 2 s to t = 3 s in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.mistake: Uses the instantaneous value at one end

quiz.q: For x = 0.1t³ (SI units), the instantaneous velocity at t = 3 s in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.mistake: Differentiates t³ as t² without multiplying by 3

quiz.q: The x–t graph of a body is a straight line sloping upward. Its instantaneous velocity
quiz.explain: A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so v is constant; an upward slope means v > 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a rising graph means rising velocity

quiz.q: At the highest point of an x–t graph shaped like a hill, the velocity is
quiz.explain: The tangent at the peak is horizontal, so the slope (velocity) is zero.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the largest position with the largest velocity

quiz.q: A car's speedometer reading is its
quiz.explain: The speedometer shows the speed at that instant.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up instantaneous and average values

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): At any instant, speed is the magnitude of velocity.
Reason (R): Over any time interval, average speed equals the magnitude of average velocity.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true for instantaneous values. R is false: if the body turns back, path length exceeds |displacement|, so average speed is larger.
quiz.mistake: Extends an instantaneous result to averages

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can you have a velocity at one single instant if no time passes?' Explain instantaneous velocity using limits and graphs.
teach.praise: Shrink the interval until it's almost nothing, and the average turns into the instantaneous velocity. Brilliant!
teach.nudge: What happens to Δx/Δt as the time interval gets very small? And what does that look like on the graph?

topics.title: Finding velocity and acceleration by differentiation

learn.hook: Give a physicist one equation for position, and two quick derivatives later she knows the velocity and acceleration at every instant.
points: If x(t) is known, v = dx/dt. Use d(tⁿ)/dt = n tⁿ⁻¹ and d(constant)/dt = 0.
Instantaneous acceleration a = dv/dt = d²x/dt²; it is the slope of the v–t graph at that instant.
For x = a + bt²: v = 2bt and acceleration = 2b (constant).
To find when the body is momentarily at rest, set v = 0 and solve for t.

example.q: x = 2.5 + 5t² (x in m, t in s). Find v and a at t = 2 s.
steps: At t = 2 s, v = 20 m s⁻¹.
example.answer: v = 20 m s⁻¹, a = 10 m s⁻²

learn.reallife: A modern train's onboard computer logs position many times a second; differentiating that data gives the speed and acceleration shown to the loco pilot.

items.q: x = t³: v at t = 2 s (m/s)

quiz.q: The position of a particle is x = 3t² − 2t + 5 (SI units). Its velocity at t = 3 s in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.mistake: Forgets the −2 term or substitutes t into x

quiz.q: For x = 3t² − 2t + 5 (SI units), the acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.explain: a = dv/dt = d(6t − 2)/dt = 6 m s⁻².
quiz.mistake: Takes the coefficient of t² as the acceleration

quiz.q: x = t³ − 6t² (SI units). At what time t (in s, t > 0) is the particle momentarily at rest?
quiz.explain: v = 3t² − 12t = 3t(t − 4) = 0 gives t = 4 s (t > 0).
quiz.mistake: Sets x = 0 instead of v = 0

quiz.q: For x = t³ − 6t² (SI units), the acceleration is zero at t (in s) =
quiz.explain: a = dv/dt = 6t − 12 = 0 gives t = 2 s.
quiz.mistake: Sets v = 0 instead of a = 0

quiz.q: Acceleration at an instant equals
options: The slope of the v–t graph at that instant
The slope of the x–t graph
The area under the v–t graph
The area under the x–t graph
quiz.explain: a = dv/dt is the slope of the tangent to the v–t curve.
quiz.mistake: Confuses slope of v–t with slope of x–t

quiz.q: For x = a + bt², which statement is correct?
options: The velocity is 2b at all times
The acceleration is constant and equal to 2b
The velocity is constant and equal to b
quiz.explain: v = 2bt and a = 2b, a constant.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 from differentiating t²

quiz.q: The velocity of a particle is v = 4t + 3t² (SI units). Its acceleration at t = 2 s in m s⁻² is
quiz.mistake: Substitutes t into v instead of differentiating

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For x = 5 + 4t (SI units), the acceleration of the particle is zero.
Reason (R): The particle starts from x = 5 m at t = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the starting position does not explain zero acceleration; the constant velocity dx/dt = 4 m s⁻¹ does.
quiz.mistake: Picks any true fact as the explanation

teach.ask: Gappu has x = 2 + 3t² and doesn't know how to get speed from it. Teach him to find velocity and acceleration.
teach.praise: Differentiate once for velocity, again for acceleration. I got v = 6t and a = 6!
teach.nudge: What mathematical step turns position into velocity? And what do you do to get acceleration?

topics.title: Acceleration: meaning, sign and x–t curvature

learn.hook: A car slowing down while reversing has a POSITIVE acceleration. Sounds wrong? It's all about the chosen direction.
points: Average acceleration = (v₂ − v₁)/(t₂ − t₁) = Δv/Δt; SI unit m s⁻².
Velocity is a vector, so acceleration arises from a change in speed, in direction, or both.
The sign of acceleration depends on the chosen positive direction; it does not by itself say 'speeding up' or 'slowing down'.
On an x–t graph: curve bending upward (slope increasing) → a > 0; bending downward → a < 0; straight line → a = 0.

example.q: A scooter's velocity changes from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. Find its average acceleration.

learn.reallife: When the Tejas jet lands at an air base and brakes hard, its acceleration points opposite to its velocity, which is why pilots lean forward.

items.text: A velocity change in direction only still means non-zero ___

quiz.q: A bus's velocity changes from 20 m s⁻¹ to 8 m s⁻¹ in 4 s (same direction, taken as +x). Its average acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.explain: a = (8 − 20)/4 = −3 m s⁻². The negative sign means acceleration is opposite to the motion (the bus slows).
quiz.mistake: Ignores the order of subtraction

quiz.q: A car moving in the −x direction is slowing down. Its acceleration is
quiz.explain: Velocity is negative and its magnitude is decreasing, so v is becoming less negative; Δv > 0 and a > 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks slowing down always means negative acceleration

quiz.q: An object moves on a circle at constant speed. Its acceleration is
options: Zero, because it returns to its start
Non-zero, because the direction of velocity changes
quiz.explain: Velocity is a vector; a change of direction alone means acceleration.
quiz.mistake: Thinks constant speed means zero acceleration

quiz.q: An x–t graph that curves upward (like a U opening upward) indicates
quiz.explain: Its slope (velocity) increases with time, so a > 0.
quiz.mistake: Reads the height of the graph instead of its bending

quiz.q: A straight-line x–t graph with negative slope represents
options: Constant negative velocity and zero acceleration
quiz.explain: A straight line has constant slope: constant velocity (negative here), so a = 0.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a negative slope with negative acceleration

quiz.q: Velocity changes from −10 m s⁻¹ to +10 m s⁻¹ in 5 s. The average acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.mistake: Treats both speeds as equal so Δv = 0

quiz.q: The SI unit of acceleration is
quiz.explain: Acceleration = velocity/time = (m s⁻¹)/s = m s⁻².
quiz.mistake: Gives the unit of velocity

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A negative acceleration always means the body is slowing down.
Reason (R): The sign of acceleration depends on the choice of positive direction.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: a body moving in −x and speeding up has negative a. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Equates 'negative acceleration' with 'deceleration'

teach.ask: Gappu thinks 'negative acceleration' always means braking. Explain what acceleration is and what its sign really tells us.
teach.praise: So the sign only tells direction, and turning also counts as acceleration. Mind blown!
teach.nudge: What does acceleration measure? And does a minus sign alone tell you the body is slowing down?

topics.title: Velocity–time graphs and the area rule

learn.hook: Give a CBSE examiner one v–t graph and they can ask you five questions: acceleration, displacement, distance, turning point and average speed.
points: On a v–t graph, slope = acceleration and area under the graph = displacement (area below the t-axis counts as negative).
Constant acceleration gives a straight-line v–t graph. If the line crosses v = 0, the body reverses direction there (e.g. a ball thrown up).
Distance travelled = sum of magnitudes of areas above and below the axis.
Real motion has no sharp kinks: x and v change continuously. Impossible graphs show two positions at one time, negative speed or path length, or time going backward.
Read graphs carefully: x–t slope gives v; v–t slope gives a, v–t area gives displacement.

example.q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m s⁻¹ in 4 s, moves steadily for 6 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 2 s. Find the total distance.

learn.reallife: Metro trains on the Delhi Metro follow a trapezium-shaped v–t profile between stations: accelerate, cruise, brake.

games.title: Physically possible graph?
items: x–t graph with a smooth curve
x–t graph with two x values at one time
x–t graph turning back in time

games.title: Reading v–t graphs
items: The area under a v–t graph gives displacement.
The slope of a v–t graph gives velocity.
Where a v–t line crosses the time axis, the body is momentarily at rest.
Area below the time axis on a v–t graph is counted as negative displacement.
A real x–t graph can have a sharp corner.
That would need an instant jump in velocity (infinite acceleration).

quiz.q: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 12 m s⁻¹ in 6 s. The area under its v–t graph, in m, is
quiz.explain: Area of triangle = ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m = displacement.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ for the triangle

quiz.q: A body accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m s⁻¹ in 6 s. Its acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.explain: Slope = 12/6 = 2 m s⁻².
quiz.mistake: Divides time by velocity

quiz.q: A v–t graph is a straight line from v = +10 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to v = −10 m s⁻¹ at t = 4 s. The displacement in 4 s, in m, is
quiz.explain: Area above the axis (½ × 2 × 10 = 10 m) cancels area below (−10 m).
quiz.mistake: Adds magnitudes, giving distance instead of displacement

quiz.q: For the same graph (+10 to −10 m s⁻¹ in 4 s), the distance travelled, in m, is
quiz.explain: Distance = 10 m + 10 m = 20 m (both areas as magnitudes).
quiz.mistake: Gives displacement instead of distance

quiz.q: A v–t graph is a straight line from +10 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to −10 m s⁻¹ at t = 4 s. The body reverses its direction at t (in s) =
quiz.explain: v becomes zero midway at t = 2 s and then turns negative.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the reversal is at the end of the graph

quiz.q: Which graph cannot represent a real one-dimensional motion?
options: A v–t graph that is a horizontal line
An x–t graph that shows two different positions at the same time
An x–t graph that is a parabola
A v–t graph crossing the time axis
quiz.explain: A body cannot be at two places at one instant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any unusual-looking graph is impossible

quiz.q: A car moves at 15 m s⁻¹ for 4 s and then brakes uniformly to rest in 3 s. The total distance, in m, is
quiz.explain: 60 m (rectangle) + ½ × 3 × 15 = 22.5 m (triangle) = 82.5 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets one part of the area

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The x–t graph of a real body cannot have a sharp kink.
Reason (R): A kink would need the velocity to change instantly, i.e. infinite acceleration.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Velocity changes continuously in real motion, so x–t graphs are smooth. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks kinks are allowed when a body stops suddenly

teach.ask: Gappu has a v–t graph and wants to know how far he flew. Explain what the slope and area of a v–t graph give, and how to spot an impossible graph.
teach.praise: Slope gives acceleration, area gives displacement, and no graph can put me in two places at once!
teach.nudge: What does the area under a v–t graph tell you? And the slope?

learn.hook: Three short equations solve almost every 'uniform acceleration' question in your board paper. Derive them once and you'll never forget them.
points: From a = (v − v₀)/t: v = v₀ + at.
Area under the v–t graph (rectangle v₀t + triangle ½(v − v₀)t = ½at²): x = v₀t + ½at².
For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (v₀ + v)/2, so x = (v₀ + v)t/2.
Eliminate t: x = (v + v₀)/2 × (v − v₀)/a gives v² = v₀² + 2ax.

example.q: A car moving at 10 m s⁻¹ accelerates at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s. Find its final velocity and displacement.
steps: Check: average velocity = (10 + 20)/2 = 15 m s⁻¹; 15 × 5 = 75 m.

learn.reallife: During an ISRO PSLV launch, engineers estimate the rocket's speed after a burn using exactly v = v₀ + at for short intervals of nearly constant acceleration.

games.title: Derive x = v₀t + ½at² from the v–t graph
items: Draw v–t line from v₀ to v over time t
Split the area into a rectangle and a triangle

games.title: Equation ↔ quantity it does NOT contain

quiz.q: A train starts from rest with acceleration 0.5 m s⁻². Its velocity after 40 s, in m s⁻¹, is
quiz.mistake: Divides instead of multiplying

quiz.q: The same train (from rest, a = 0.5 m s⁻²) covers how many metres in 40 s?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ or the square

quiz.q: A car accelerates from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ over 100 m. Its acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.mistake: Uses (v − v₀)/x

quiz.q: A body moving with uniform acceleration has initial velocity 6 m s⁻¹ and final velocity 14 m s⁻¹ after 4 s. Its displacement, in m, is
quiz.mistake: Uses only the final velocity × time

quiz.q: Which equation is obtained by eliminating time from the other two?
quiz.explain: Using t = (v − v₀)/a in x = (v + v₀)t/2 gives v² = v₀² + 2ax.
quiz.mistake: Picks an equation that still contains t

quiz.q: In deriving x = v₀t + ½at² from the v–t graph, the term ½at² is the area of the
quiz.explain: The triangle has base t and height (v − v₀) = at, so its area is ½at².
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two parts of the area

quiz.q: For uniformly accelerated motion, average velocity equals (v₀ + v)/2 because
options: The body always starts from rest
quiz.explain: With constant a, v rises linearly, so the time-average is the simple mean of the end values.
quiz.mistake: Applies (v₀ + v)/2 to every kind of motion

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): v² = v₀² + 2ax does not contain time.
Reason (R): It is obtained by eliminating t between v = v₀ + at and x = (v₀ + v)t/2.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Eliminating t is exactly how the third equation is derived. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the equations are independent of each other

teach.ask: Gappu memorised v² = v₀² + 2ax but has no idea where it comes from. Show him how the three kinematic equations are derived.
teach.praise: One from the definition, one from the area, and one by kicking out time. I'll never forget them now!
teach.nudge: Where does the first equation come from? And how can a graph's area give the second?

topics.title: General forms, calculus method and when the equations work

learn.hook: Toss a cricket ball straight up: at the top it has zero velocity for an instant, yet gravity is still pulling it at 9.8 m s⁻². Zero velocity, non-zero acceleration!
points: With initial position x₀: x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² and v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀).
Calculus: a = dv/dt → ∫dv = ∫a dt → v = v₀ + at; v = dx/dt → ∫dx = ∫(v₀ + at)dt → x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at². Also v dv/dx = a gives v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀).
These equations hold ONLY for constant acceleration. The definitions v = dx/dt and a = dv/dt hold always.
Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration (top of a vertical throw). Speeding up or slowing down depends on whether a and v have the same or opposite signs.

example.q: A particle at x₀ = 5 m has v₀ = 3 m s⁻¹ and a = 2 m s⁻². Find its position at t = 4 s.

learn.reallife: Self-driving test cars at IIT Madras's research park model braking with these equations only after checking that the deceleration is roughly constant.

games.title: When do the equations apply?
items: x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² is valid when acceleration varies with time.
v = dx/dt is valid for any motion.
At the highest point of a vertical throw, v = 0 but a = −g.
If a is negative, the body is always slowing down.
It speeds up if v is also negative.
Integrating a = dv/dt with constant a gives v = v₀ + at.

quiz.q: A particle starts at x₀ = −4 m with v₀ = 6 m s⁻¹ and a = −2 m s⁻². Its position at t = 2 s, in m, is
quiz.mistake: Forgets x₀ or the sign of a

quiz.q: Which relation remains valid even when acceleration is not constant?
quiz.explain: dx/dt is the definition of velocity and applies always; the others assume constant a.
quiz.mistake: Uses kinematic equations for variable acceleration

quiz.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward. At its highest point
options: Velocity is zero but acceleration is g downward
Both velocity and acceleration are zero
Acceleration is zero but velocity is not
quiz.explain: The ball is momentarily at rest, but gravity still accelerates it downward at g.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero velocity implies zero acceleration

quiz.q: A body has v = −5 m s⁻¹ and a = −2 m s⁻². It is
quiz.explain: a and v have the same sign, so the speed increases.
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative acceleration always slows a body

quiz.q: For a = 6t (variable), a student uses v = v₀ + at to find v. The mistake is
options: The equation needs constant acceleration; here v = v₀ + 3t² by integration
quiz.explain: Integrating a = 6t gives v = v₀ + 3t²; v = v₀ + at is only for constant a.
quiz.mistake: Applies constant-acceleration formulas to variable acceleration

quiz.q: A car at x₀ = 10 m moves with v₀ = 4 m s⁻¹ and a = 2 m s⁻². Its velocity when it reaches x = 22 m, in m s⁻¹, is
quiz.mistake: Uses x instead of (x − x₀) or forgets the square root

quiz.q: The equation v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀) can be derived by calculus using
quiz.explain: a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx; integrating v dv = a dx gives the result.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the chain-rule form of acceleration

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A body can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration at the same instant.
Reason (R): At the topmost point of vertical motion under gravity, v = 0 while a = g downward.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The top of a throw is a classic example of A, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rest means no acceleration

teach.ask: Gappu used v = v₀ + at for a rocket whose acceleration keeps rising, and thinks a = 0 at the top of a throw. Correct him.
teach.praise: So the three equations need constant a, and the top of a throw still has gravity. Thanks for saving my maths!
teach.nudge: When are the kinematic equations allowed? And what is the acceleration at the top of a throw?

topics.title: Free fall and Galileo's odd-number rule

learn.hook: Drop a stone from Qutub Minar's top (about 72.5 m) and gravity takes under 4 seconds to bring it down. Air resistance aside, a feather would do the same.
points: Free fall: motion under gravity alone with constant acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward (ignoring air resistance).
Take upward as +y: a = −g. Then v = v₀ − gt, y = v₀t − ½gt², v² = v₀² − 2gy.
A ball thrown up and landing below the launch point: solve the whole flight with one equation (y negative at landing) or split it into 'up' and 'down' parts — both give the same time.
Galileo's law of odd numbers: for a body falling from rest, distances in successive equal time intervals are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 …

example.q: A ball is thrown up at 10 m s⁻¹ from the top of a 15 m building (g = 10 m s⁻²). How long does it take to reach the ground?
steps: Take up as +, origin at the top: landing y = −15 m.
Check by splitting: up for 1 s rising 5 m, then falls 20 m in 2 s: total 3 s.

learn.reallife: Paragliders over Bir Billing feel close to free fall for a moment after jumping, before the canopy fills with air.

quiz.q: A stone is dropped from rest. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², its speed after 2 s in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.mistake: Uses ½gt² (distance) instead of gt

quiz.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 19.6 m s⁻¹ (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The maximum height reached, in m, is
quiz.explain: At the top v = 0: h = v₀²/2g = 19.6²/19.6 = 19.6 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 in 2g

quiz.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 19.6 m s⁻¹ (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The time to reach the top in s is
quiz.mistake: Gives the total time of flight

quiz.q: A ball is thrown up at 20 m s⁻¹ from the top of a 25 m tower (g = 10 m s⁻²). Taking up as positive, the equation for the time t to hit the ground is
quiz.explain: With origin at the top and up positive, the ground is at y = −25 m and a = −10 m s⁻².
quiz.mistake: Takes landing displacement as +25 m

quiz.q: A ball thrown up at 20 m s⁻¹ from a 25 m tower (g = 10 m s⁻²) lands when −25 = 20t − 5t². The time to hit the ground in s is
steps: t = 5 s or −1 s; take 5 s
quiz.mistake: Keeps the negative root

quiz.q: A body falls from rest. The distances covered in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds are in the ratio
quiz.explain: Total distances go as 1 : 4 : 9 (t²), so distances in successive seconds are 1 : 3 : 5.
quiz.mistake: Gives the ratio of total distances (1 : 4 : 9)

quiz.q: With g = 10 m s⁻², the distance a body falling from rest covers during the 3rd second, in m, is
quiz.explain: Distance in 3 s = 45 m, in 2 s = 20 m, so during the 3rd second = 25 m.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total distance in 3 s

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In free fall, a body moving upward has an upward acceleration.
Reason (R): Near the Earth's surface, gravity gives every freely moving body an acceleration g directed downward.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: the acceleration is g downward even while the body rises (it is slowing down). R is true.
quiz.mistake: Thinks acceleration points along the motion

teach.ask: Gappu thinks a ball's acceleration is upward while it rises and zero at the top. Explain free fall and the sign convention.
teach.praise: Gravity points down the whole time, up, top and down. I'll take up as positive and use a = −g!
teach.nudge: Which way does gravity accelerate the ball while it is going up? What value and sign do you use?

topics.title: Stopping distance, reaction time and kinematics numericals

learn.hook: Double your speed on a highway and your braking distance becomes FOUR times longer. That single fact is why speed limits exist.
points: Braking from v₀ with deceleration a: 0 = v₀² − 2a·d_s, so stopping distance d_s = v₀²/(2a) ∝ v₀².
Reaction time with a falling ruler: the ruler falls d = ½gt² before you catch it, so t = √(2d/g).
Strategy: list known quantities (v₀, v, a, x, t) with signs, pick the equation that contains the unknown and three knowns.
Units first: convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ (divide by 3.6) before using the equations.

example.q: A friend drops a ruler and you catch it after it falls 19.6 cm (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find your reaction time.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways' signal spacing depends on braking distance: a train at 90 km h⁻¹ needs far more track to stop than one at 45 km h⁻¹.

games.title: Situation ↔ equation to use
pairs: Find time to stop from v₀ with deceleration a
Find distance fallen from rest in time t
Find reaction time from ruler drop d

items.q: Stop from 20 m/s at 5 m/s²: time (s)
Stop from 20 m/s at 5 m/s²: distance (m)
Speed doubled: stopping distance becomes how many times

quiz.q: A car moving at 72 km h⁻¹ brakes with a uniform retardation of 4 m s⁻². Its stopping distance in m is
quiz.mistake: Uses 72 directly without converting to m s⁻¹

quiz.q: If the car's initial speed is tripled (same retardation), its stopping distance becomes how many times larger?
quiz.explain: d ∝ v₀², so tripling v₀ multiplies d by 9.
quiz.mistake: Thinks stopping distance is proportional to speed

quiz.q: A ruler is caught after falling 44.1 cm (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The reaction time in s is
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root

quiz.q: A train at 20 m s⁻¹ applies brakes and stops in 10 s with uniform retardation. The distance covered while braking, in m, is
quiz.explain: Average velocity = (20 + 0)/2 = 10 m s⁻¹, distance = 10 × 10 = 100 m.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies initial speed by time

quiz.q: A stone is dropped from a 44.1 m high cliff (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The time to reach the ground in s is
quiz.mistake: Forgets the square root

quiz.q: The stone dropped from 44.1 m hits the ground with speed (m s⁻¹)
quiz.mistake: Uses the height as the speed

quiz.q: A bike accelerates from rest at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s, then moves at constant velocity for 10 s. The total distance in m is
quiz.explain: First phase: ½ × 2 × 25 = 25 m, reaching 10 m s⁻¹. Second: 10 × 10 = 100 m. Total 125 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the first phase or the second

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Stopping distance of a vehicle is proportional to the square of its initial speed (constant retardation).
Reason (R): Stopping distance does not depend on the braking retardation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true since d = v₀²/(2a). R is false: a larger retardation a gives a smaller d.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the role of braking force

teach.ask: Gappu's uncle says driving at 80 km/h instead of 40 km/h only doubles the braking distance. Explain why he is wrong, and how a ruler can measure reaction time.
teach.praise: Double the speed, four times the distance! And the ruler trick turns gravity into a stopwatch.
teach.nudge: How does stopping distance depend on speed? Which equation shows it?
